title: Systematic Alpha Discovery in Foreign Exchange Markets A Two-phase Research Program: From Exhaustive Structural-factor Search to Fundamentals-Driven Machine Learning
abstract: This paper documents a two-phase research program to identify statistically defensible trading edges in foreign exchange markets. Phase I conducted an exhaustive, rule-based search for structural and fundamental factors-real yield differentials, Commitment of Traders (COT) positioning, sessionbased liquidity patterns, and inter-market correlations-explicitly excluding conventional technical indicators, and subjected 18,681 candidate strategy/parameter combinations across 22 research phases to a four-stage validation gauntlet (in-sample/walk-forward testing, Monte Carlo Permutation Testing, Bonferroni correction, and the Deflated Sharpe Ratio). Zero candidates passed the complete gauntlet, a null result interpreted as evidence of the pipeline's capacity to reject data-mined artifacts rather than a failure of the research program. Informed by this result and by a review of external reference material, the program subsequently evolved into Phase II: a fundamentals-driven machine learning architecture combining gradient-boosted ensemble models (LightGBM, XGBoost, Random Forest) trained on macroeconomic (FRED) and cross-asset (Yahoo Finance) data, hidden Markov model-based regime-strict filtering, walk-forward cross-validation, and a production deployment layer with explicit risk controls. This paper documents both phases, compares their methodological standards-including a materially different statistical significance threshold between phases-and outlines the audits and extensions needed before any Phase II strategy is promoted to live trading.
why: Rigorous FX alpha search, null result validates rejection method

title: Asymmetric Volatility Transmission Between AI Compute Infrastructure and Regional Power Grids: Evidence from Quantile Connectedness Under Extreme Market States
abstract: The rapid deployment of artificial-intelligence (AI) models has transformed data centers from relatively passive consumers of electricity into geographically concentrated, high-density loads whose investment cycles increasingly intersect with wholesale electricity markets. In this paper we examine whether volatility spillovers between AI-compute infrastructure, regional power grids, energy commodities, utilities and general financial risk are asymmetric across market states. The study uses a daily 2020–2026 framework and a quantile vector autoregression (QVAR) connectedness system, differentiating lower-tail (q = 0.05), median (q = 0.50), and upper-tail (q = 0.95) dependence. The empirical design includes an AI-compute equity basket, data-center real-estate investment trusts, PJM and ERCOT wholesale electricity prices, natural-gas futures, uranium/nuclear equities, the U.S. utilities sector, Nasdaq-100 returns and the VIX. The empirical results show a much stronger system-wide dependence in the lower tail compared to the conditional median: total connectedness is approximately 68.7% at q = 0.05, 48.9% at q = 0.50 and 61.8% at q = 0.95. This asymmetry is not only due to higher volatility, but also to the change in the direction of transmission. Ordinary expansion results in larger net receivers of technology shocks in regional electricity prices, and PJM/ERCOT and natural gas become stronger transmitters during stress states. AI-compute equities and data-center REITs also have different tail roles, which is consistent with the interaction of expectations for future compute capacity and physical constraints on electricity supply. Dynamic estimates show spikes in connectedness at pandemic-reopening, 2022 energy shock, large AI-product cycles and subsequent data-center load-planning revisions. The results support a risk monitoring that embraces financial and physical-energy variables jointly, instead of regarding data-center expansion as a concern of the technology sector only.
why: AI compute-power grid volatility spillover, real network signal

title: How To Forecast Volatility of Crypto Derivatives When Data History (Implied Vol.) Is Limited? Would the Traditional Econometric Models Work?
abstract: This study examines the effectiveness of traditional econometric models, such as ARMA, GARCH, and EGARCH, in forecasting the implied volatility of crypto derivatives when data history is limited. We compare these models with machine learning approaches, including LASSO and Gradient Boosting, which utilize additional features like returns and rolling volatility. The results show that simpler models like ARMA and LASSO outperform GARCH-based models, which struggle with limited data. Machine learning models demonstrate competitive performance, highlighting their adaptability to the unique characteristics of cryptocurrency markets. These findings provide valuable insights into selecting appropriate forecasting methods for crypto derivatives under data constraints.
why: Crypto IV forecasting actionable, evaluation rigor not detailed

title: Explainable Machine Learning Model for Credit Default Risk Prediction Using Lending Club Loan Data with Shap Analysis and Risk Segmentation
abstract: Credit risk assessment is fundamental to lending profitability and portfolio quality. Traditional models often fail to capture non‑linear borrower behaviours, while complex machine learning models remain difficult to interpret. This study develops an explainable machine learning pipeline to predict loan defaults using Lending Club data, addressing both predictive accuracy and business transparency. Following a structured analytics workflow – data cleaning, feature selection via SelectKBest, stratified train‑test splitting, and SMOTE‑based resampling – three classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost) are trained and evaluated. Rather than relying on accuracy alone (which is misleading in imbalanced datasets), models are compared using precision, recall, F1‑score, and ROC‑AUC. SHAP analysis provides global and local interpretability. Results show that XGBoost achieves the strongest performance (ROC‑AUC = 0.996), and SHAP reveals that payment history and outstanding principal – not static application features – are the most influential drivers of default risk. This work demonstrates that high‑performance models need not be “black boxes”; with appropriate explanation tools, lending institutions can adopt sophisticated analytics while maintaining regulatory accountability and stakeholder trust.
why: Standard ML pipeline, public dataset, no novelty or surprise

title: Speed Limits for Liquidity: Queues, Gates, and Runs in Semi-Liquid Funds
abstract: Semi-liquid funds-non-traded BDCs, interval and tender-offer funds-repurchase shares each quarter at net asset value up to a cap, typically 5% of shares, and ration excess requests pro rata. We develop an equilibrium model of this mechanism. A cap works as a speed limit. If the drain it permits, 𝜅[𝜃 + Λ(1 + 𝜃)], does not exceed the fund's excess return plus costless liquidity, 𝜋 + Λ𝜇, no investor base can run the fund. Above this floor, runs are sustained by the backlog of liquidity-constrained investors they trap in the queue. We characterise the run region in closed form, show that a backlog above a tipping level eliminates the no-run equilibrium, and show that tighter caps can be more fragile. We then characterise all run-proof designs. Among work-conserving anonymous rules, a fund is robust to every investor base if and only if its cap satisfies the speed limit-most cheaply implemented through a fee we show to be minimal-or all liquidity needs are verified and prioritised and requests are withdrawable. Irrevocable, first-in-first-out and last-in-first-out queues are more fragile than withdrawable pro rata, and leverage lowers the floor. Tender-offer filings for 46 funds show that proration, absent in private-credit BDCs before 2026, reached 23% of their offers in 2026 and is highly persistent. AI disclosure: This paper was prepared with substantial assistance from a large language model (Claude, Anthropic). The author's and the AI system's roles are described in the Declarations section. The author takes full responsibility for the content.
why: Theoretical fund equilibrium analysis, no empirical test

title: Generative Ethics: How AI Model Choice Shapes Social and Financial Performance
abstract: This paper estimates potential effects of AI adoption on firms' ethical decision making. Here I focus on variation in models' partiality, defined as the weight given to the party it serves relative to a third party. Study 1 applies an established instrument from computer science, administering 5,000 autonomous-vehicle dilemmas to each of fifteen frontier models and recovering a measure of moral partiality. Models differ sharply. All favor third parties over their principal, but by very different amounts. Some are nearly indifferent, while others will let up to five passengers die rather than kill a single pedestrian. Study 2 casts the same models as business advisors choosing, across 260 pairs, between projected firm revenue and jobs created outside the firm. From each model's choices, I estimate how much revenue it will give up per job. Twelve models pay for community employment, at rates from $923 to $7,066 per job; two place no measurable weight on it; and one, xAI's Grok, requires additional revenue before it will accept community jobs at all. Partiality in the vehicle dilemmas predicts how much revenue models give up for community jobs (ρ = .725, p = .002). AI thus introduces a new source of variation in how firms balance their objectives, and which model a firm adopts is a decision about whose interests the organization will prioritize.
why: LLM ethics outcomes, unclear mechanism or implementability

title: Environmental Externalities from Technological Investment: Voluntary Disclosure and the Market Response to Datacenter News
abstract: Although technological investment has become increasingly critical to firm value, firms' artificial intelligence ("AI") activities are largely unobservable to investors. While managers have strong incentives to communicate the economic benefits of AI investment, the decision to inform investors about negative externalities caused by these investments is less clear. We examine whether and how firms discuss environmental issues in the context of their datacenter investments, and whether these disclosures are associated with analyst and investor responses to firm datacenter disclosure. We provide consistent evidence that firms increase environmental disclosure in conjunction with discussion of datacenter investment, on average. On average, our sample firms increase positive and forward-looking environmental disclosure in conjunction with datacenter mentions. However, increases in negative and risk-specific environmental disclosure are concentrated in AI firms, while increases in historical environmental disclosure are concentrated in non-AI firms. Finally, we provide evidence that in the presence of datacenter investment disclosure, analysts ask fewer negative environmental questions and investors in AI firms react more strongly to earnings and forecast news. Overall, this suggests that environmental disclosure helps provide a more complete economic picture of firms' datacenter investments. * The authors are grateful for helpful comments from Gabe Brull, Sean Cao and Rui Shen. All errors are our own.
why: Datacenter disclosure event study, not method to implement

title: Post-Consultation Position Paper: Attribution Infrastructure for Autonomous Financial Agents
abstract: When an autonomous financial agent makes a consequential decision, three questions must be answerable retroactively: which agent acted, was it operating within its authorized scope, and is there a verifiable record? The challenge compounds in multi-hop delegation chains, where a human authorizes Agent1, which in turn delegates to Agent2. In these H2A2A (Human-to-Agent-to-Agent) configurations, no existing regulatory framework specifies which principal bears accountability at each delegation hop, or what calibration requirements govern agents that receive delegated authority rather than direct human authorization. The Financial Stability Board's June 2026 consultation on Sound Practices for Responsible AI Adoption (P100626) requires all three attribution elements but specifies no technical protocol for how they are cryptographically authenticated and transmitted to supervisors. The resulting gap is not organizational. It is infrastructural. This paper names and analyzes that gap. The core distinction it introduces is between data-layer attribution (proving a record was not modified after issuance) and authorization-chain attribution (proving an agent was authorized to act within scope at the time of a specific decision). These are different infrastructure requirements; the first is largely solved by blockchain and cryptographic hashing; the second has no established standard. Analysis of thirteen regulatory documents spanning six geographic jurisdictions confirms that Multi-Agent Attribution (the specification of accountability for delegated authorization chains) scores 0/12 across all Category A governance frameworks (pre-adjudication inter-rater reliability κ = 0.6507). The proposed framework, AIF v0.1, addresses authorization-chain attribution through three components: W3C Decentralized Identifier and Verifiable Credential specifications for agent identity and delegation-chain attestation, and a 13-field Calibration Reporting Standard (CRS) applying privacy-preserving verification to calibration governance disclosures. The framework is grounded in practitioner evidence from three operational contexts: autonomous content policy enforcement at Meta (2017-2019), e-invoicing attribution infrastructure at a digital asset infrastructure organization in Abu Dhabi (2026), and autonomous fraud and Sybil detection at OKX (2023-2024). An implementation path for FSB member jurisdictions is proposed, with a proportionality mechanism tied to the materiality assessment framework in Sound Practice 5.
why: Position paper, regulatory framework, not technical solution

title: One Right Question is Worth a Thousand Pages: Question Capital, Cognitive Compression, and the Reorganization of Expertise in an Age of Answer Abundance
abstract: Generative AI has sharply reduced the marginal cost of obtaining explanations, summaries, drafts, comparisons, and plausible answers. This paper argues that such answer abundance does not eliminate cognitive inequality; it changes its location. When answers become cheaper, the scarce resource may increasingly be the human capacity to identify what is worth asking, to re-represent a problem, and to formulate questions that expose hidden structure. I refer to this capacity here as question capital. Question capital is not prompt fluency and is not attributed to AI. It is a human capacity to detect epistemic gaps, choose high-leverage contrasts, construct counterfactual removals, locate boundaries, identify invariants, build structural analogies, and formulate falsifying questions. The paper develops a sociology of question capital and a companion concept, cognitive compression: the reduction of a large information burden into a compact relational model without discarding the structure needed for explanation and transfer. A family of question operators is formalized and illustrated through examples ranging from removing electrons from a hypothetical universe to subtracting an organizational closure variable Pi, removing a possibility variable Psi, comparing distributed galaxy emergence with nucleation in boiling water, and asking what remains of a profession when credentials are removed but demonstrated competence persists. The paper then derives testable propositions about expertise, education, inequality, credentialing, and human-AI work. A controlled question-architecture experiment is specified to test whether structural questioning produces greater transfer, faster model formation, and lower information consumption than retrieval-oriented questioning under the same AI, time, and source-material conditions. The central claim is deliberately limited: AI may make answers abundant, but it does not own the human act of deciding which question is worth asking. As answer costs fall, the social value of question formation may rise.
why: Philosophical essay, not actionable for financial systems.

title: Beyond Historical Mean Returns: A Long Short-Term Memory Approach to Portfolio Optimisation on the Malawi Stock Exchange
abstract: Investors on the Malawi Stock Exchange face a frustrating problem: the standard tools for building a portfolio assume that the past is a reliable indicator, yet in a small market shaken by currency devaluations and policy shifts, yesterday's averages can mislead. This paper asks a simple question. What happens if, instead of feeding the classical Markowitz model long-run historical averages, we give it a forecast that pays attention to what the market has been doing lately? We use a neural network suited to time-series data (Long Short-Term Memory, or LSTM) to produce these forecasts, show mathematically that the combined model is sound and stable, and test it on eight years of monthly prices for all sixteen listed Malawian companies, keeping the final eighteen months completely untouched for an honest evaluation. The market showed substantial variation across stocks, with average monthly returns from 0.5% to 5.8% over the estimation period and several banking stocks repricing by more than 50% within a few months of the November 2023 kwacha devaluation. The results are encouraging: the prediction-based portfolio earned more than the classical one, a cumulative return of 275 % compared with 195 % over the hold-out period, with a better return for the risk taken and, notably, slightly less volatility. Even simpler forecasting rules improved on the classical model, which points to the real lesson. In markets like Malawi's, how you estimate expected returns matters more than the optimisation model itself. Everything, from data to results, can be replicated from our published code.
why: Single-market LSTM, judge rejects non-transferable country empirics

title: A Novel Hybrid Approach Combining Re-decomposition and Frequency-Specific Modeling for Stock Index Forecasting
abstract: Stock price forecasting is a key aspect of investment decision-making and risk management. Since stock price series are often nonlinear and nonstationary, accurately forecasting stock prices remains a challenging task. To address this issue, this study proposes a novel hybrid deep learning model. Improved Complete Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition with Adaptive Noise (ICEEMDAN) is employed for the initial decomposition of the stock index closing price series to separate information at different time scales. Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) is used to re-decompose the highest-frequency component obtained from the initial decomposition, thereby reducing its complexity. A Genetic Algorithm (GA) is employed to optimize the VMD parameters to improve the decomposition performance. The Informer model is used to capture rapid variation patterns in the high-frequency components (H-IMFs), while the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model is employed to capture long-term dependencies in the low-frequency components (L-IMFs). The proposed hybrid model is named the ICEEMDAN-GA-VMD-Informer-LSTM model.In the empirical study, the CSI 300 Index is used as the dataset. By comparing the proposed model with several benchmark models, it is demonstrated that the ICEEMDAN-GA-VMD-Informer-LSTM model achieves the best forecasting performance. The ablation study shows that each component of the proposed model makes a significant contribution to the overall forecasting performance. Multi-step forecasting experiment, the MCS test, and substitute dataset experiment demonstrate that the proposed model has good robustness. These results highlight the application potential of hybrid deep learning models in the stock market and provide useful guidance for investors and regulatory.
why: Stock predictor method-stacking, no rigor or baselines shown

title: Public Debt, Wealth Inequality, and the Burden of Taxation
abstract: Public debt and wealth concentration have co-moved persistently across advanced economies and historical periods, defying standard theories of wealth inequality, particularly given that rising inequality has coincided with falling real interest rates in recent decades. I develop a stylized Diamond model with household heterogeneity and progressive taxation to formalize how public debt, through its tax burden, endogenously dictates tax progressivity and thereby affects the wealth distribution. In this framework, permanent debt shocks alter tax progressivity depending on the macroeconomic regime, with debt expansions increasing progressivity when interest rates are high but reducing it when interest rates are low. The resulting impact of public debt on wealth inequality is nonlinear in the overall level of the tax burden, disequalizing below a threshold and equalizing above it. Cross-country empirical evidence supports these predictions and shows that public debt is a quantitatively important, and often dominant, driver of postwar wealth inequality, with sizable effects transmitted primarily through the tax burden. These findings establish the distribution of the tax burden as a primary driver of long-run wealth inequality, and public debt as a central mediating channel through which structural shocks, such as population aging or artificial intelligence, propagate to the wealth distribution.
why: Pure macro theory, no implementation or financial data.

title: "The Role of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in Developing Digital Management Accounting and Achieving Public Spending Efficiency in the Syrian Arab Republic"
abstract: The purpose of this research was to explain the role of artificial intelligence technologies in the development of digital management accounting and achieving the efficiency of public expenditure in the Syrian Arab Republic, while revealing the nature of the relationship between variables, testing the impact of these technologies, and knowing the differences in the perception of employees according to their academic qualification and years of experience. The study adopted the descriptive-analytical method, and applied an electronic questionnaire to a simple random sample of employees in the financial and accounting departments in a number of Syrian public entities, which reached (198) valid questionnaires out of (220), with a response rate of (90%). Data were analysed using SPSS, descriptive statistical methods, Cronbach's alpha coefficient, regression analysis, Pearson correlation coefficient, T-test, and univariate analysis. The results showed that there is a statistically significant effect of artificial intelligence technologies on the development of digital management accounting, as they explained (55.1%) of the change, and on the efficiency of public expenditure with an explanatory ratio (46.9%). There was also a strong direct relationship between the development of digital management accounting and the efficiency of public expenditure amounting to (0.718). Significant differences appeared according to the scientific qualification in favor of postgraduate studies, without differences attributable to years of experience. It concluded that there is a gap between theoretical perception and the reality of application due to the weakness of infrastructure, lack of qualification and inadequacy of legislation. It recommended building a national strategy for digital transformation, infrastructure development, qualifying cadres, updating legislative frameworks, and integrating artificial intelligence in budget preparation and expenditure control.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Real Estate Market Forecasting and Demand Prediction: A Narrative Review
abstract: Real estate markets are characterized by heterogeneous assets, infrequent transactions, and delayed price discovery, all of which complicate forecasting and demand estimation. This paper reviews the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in real estate market forecasting and demand prediction. Using a narrative review design, it synthesizes evidence on data sources, modeling approaches, and applications, and evaluates them against five criteria: predictive accuracy, timeliness, interpretability, data requirements, and fairness risk. The synthesis indicates that, in many studies, ensemble tree methods improve out-of-sample price prediction relative to linear hedonic models; that alternative data such as online search activity and imagery can add early information about demand; and that deep learning is most valuable for image, text, and long time-series inputs. However, performance gains depend on data quality and stable market conditions, as illustrated by the 2021 closure of Zillow Offers. Persistent challenges include regime change, limited explainability, algorithmic bias, and feedback effects. The paper proposes a practical framework for adoption based on benchmarking, uncertainty quantification, continuous monitoring, and human oversight, and identifies research priorities for data-scarce markets.
why: Literature review narrative synthesis only, rejected category

title: AI as intensifier: Digital Dualism, State Capacity, and the Stock-Flow Problem
abstract: We argue that consequential effects of AI on the global political economy are already observable, and they follow from a structural shift in the character of technological dependency. Historically, technology transferred to developing countries constituted a stock, a domestically held asset that could be inspected, worked with, learned from, and absorbed through sustained engagement. Frontier AI, by contrast, is consumed as a flow, continuous and externally controlled, foreclosing the learning process and inhibiting capability accumulation. We argue that this shift changes what dependency means for state capacity, in ways that classical dependency and development state theories do not anticipate. The argument is developed though digital dualism, a framework characterizing platform capitalism's effects on accumulation, labour, and the state in Global South economies. We find that the four mechanisms underlying digital dualism cohere under a single upstream/downstream logic under AI: concentrated control of the technology stack upstream shapes the terms on which labour and value are extracted downstream. This sharpens the state's structural double bind-its position as both necessary counterweight to digital capital and the actor most eroded by it-through a mechanism where the two horns are causally entangled. We study the case of China, whose partial success in building domestic AI capability illustrates the dependency's layered structure. We also develop the implications for economic outcomes under digital dualism, with AI intensification likely to worsen the development trap, widen the dual economy, deepen oligarchy, and raise the bar for realizing the developmental state.
why: Development economics, state capacity, no financial ML relevance

title: Whose Knowledge becomes Visible: Information Access and Equity in Hybrid Work at Microsoft
abstract: Organizational research on hybrid work has largely treated proximity bias as a behavioral or managerial failure — a bias to be corrected through leadership training or policy redesign. This paper argues that proximity bias is better understood as an information-equity problem: a structural asymmetry in who has access to the informal, high-bandwidth channels through which trust, opportunity, and organizational knowledge actually circulate. Using Microsoft's 2022-2024 hybrid work transition as a case, this paper traces how formal communication infrastructure — meetings, memos, digital collaboration tools — systematically fails to carry the same information that in-person, informal channels do, producing measurable disparities in visibility and advancement between co-located and remote employees. Drawing on information behavior theory alongside organizational behavior frameworks, the paper reframes two commonly proposed interventions, participative decision-making and structural redesign, as information-channel interventions rather than purely managerial ones, asking of each whether it redistributes access to information or merely reorganizes who delivers it. The paper closes by situating this case within a broader question: as organizations increasingly route information through AI-mediated systems, will those systems inherit, correct, or obscure the same access asymmetries that shaped Microsoft's hybrid transition.

title: Support Of Sellers After Attacks On Marketplaces; Tax On Large Ai Models To Fund New Jobs; Redistrinution Of Access Platform Revenues In Favor Of New Publishers
abstract: This paper focuses on current changes in the regulation of the digital economy and new approaches to the distribution of risks and revenues arising from the development of digital platforms and artificial intelligence. The paper focuses on three main topics: support for marketplace sellers affected by drone attacks, protecting jobs in the face of automation, and redistributing revenue from digital platforms in favor of content creators. With regard to platform-based commerce, the paper examines support measures for Wildberries and Ozon sellers whose goods were damaged as a result of drone attacks, including tax deferrals, compensation, and incentives provided by the marketplaces. The paper analyzes the specifics of determining the extent of damage and the allocation of liability among the platform, the seller, the insurer, and the state. The Russian approach is compared with foreign mechanisms for compensating businesses for losses resulting from military and terrorist risks, and the possibility of establishing a permanent insurance system and government participation in covering such losses is also examined. With regard to the regulation of artificial intelligence, the article analyzes new initiatives in the United States and Brazil aimed at mitigating the impact of automation on the labor market. It examines proposals to introduce taxes and mandatory contributions for AI developers and companies that replace workers with technology, with the proceeds directed toward retraining and the creation of new jobs. Special attention is given to measures to encourage the hiring of workers who have lost their jobs due to automation, as well as to the challenge of establishing a link between the adoption of AI and job losses. The paper also examines the trend toward redistributing revenue from the largest digital platforms in favor of content creators. Using Australia as an example, it analyzes a new mechanism for levying a levy on major media platforms and search engines to fund news publications. The Australian approach is compared with mechanisms for compensating publishers in Italy and for funding national audiovisual production in the EU. The paper also separately assesses the possibility of applying similar tools to support the media and other creative industries whose revenues are declining due to changes in content consumption patterns driven by digital platforms and AI.
why: Russian marketplace policy analysis, not quantitative finance
